# Formal logic (valid deduction and fallacies) (`formal_logic`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, boolean_logic
- Core idea: An argument is valid when its form guarantees that the conclusion is true if the premises are, whatever it is about: 'all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C'; 'if P then Q, and P, so Q'. Validity is separate from truth, so a valid argument with a false premise proves nothing, and logic alone gives no new facts about the world, only what is already contained in the premises. The practical use is to spot the common invalid forms: 'if P then Q, and Q, so P' (affirming the consequent, the form of most 'the omen came true' reasoning). Distinguish formal invalidity from defects such as assuming the very claim at issue: a circular argument can be valid but gives no independent reason to believe it. In Greek, Indian, Islamic and scholastic settings the audience already knows this art well, so the player gains by using it correctly rather than by teaching it.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing valid with true, or thinking logic can settle questions of fact without observation
  - Lecturing a 15th-century university audience on syllogisms they know far better than the player
  - Calling every disliked argument a 'fallacy'; appeal to a qualified authority or to experience is not one
  - Claiming Aristotle's logic was wrong; it was correct but covered only part of what Stoic and modern logic handle
- History: greece: c. 350 BC – Aristotle's syllogistic (Prior Analytics); 3rd c. BC Chrysippus's propositional logic; india: early centuries AD (dating disputed) – Nyaya five-membered inference; c. 500 AD Dignaga's Buddhist logic; c. 13th–14th c. Gangesa develops Navya-Nyaya; china: c. 300 BC – Later Mohist Canons on definition, inference and disputation; the school fades from view in the early imperial period; islamic: 10th–11th c. – al-Farabi and Ibn Sina extend Aristotle with conditional and temporal logic; logic enters the madrasa curriculum; europe: 12th–14th c. – scholastic logic (Abelard, Peter of Spain, Ockham, Buridan); 1847–1854 Boole's algebra of logic; 1879 Frege's predicate logic
- Read:
  - Aristotle, Prior Analytics (c. 350 BC)
  - William Kneale & Martha Kneale, The Development of Logic (1962)
  - A. C. Graham, Later Mohist Logic, Ethics and Science (1978)
